query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of tungsten (2–5 at%) to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy without tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents along with other elements (each within 5–35 at%), processed without tungsten.
generation.intervention: Incorporate 2–5 at% tungsten into the alloy during melting and processing.
generation.conditions: Heat-treatment and mechanical testing under identical protocols at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–1000°C).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of tungsten-enriched precipitates and refinement of the grain structure, especially at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten’s high melting point and limited solubility promote the formation of secondary phases that pin grain boundaries and impede dislocation motion, thereby reducing mechanisms such as creep and softening at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature yield strength and reduced creep strain, with improvements on the approximate order of 15–20% relative to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy processed without tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for tungsten additions within 2–5 at% and for mechanical testing conducted at temperatures ranging from 700°C to 1000°C; effects outside these parameters are not defined.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement and microstructural influence require experimental confirmation, and inherent variability in processing may affect the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same base titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy using identical processing protocols: one set with a 2–5 at% tungsten addition and one without. Subject both sets to the same heat treatment and perform tensile and creep tests at a representative high temperature (e.g., 800°C).
measurements: Creep strain under elevated temperature over a defined period
Microstructural analysis (e.g., electron microscopy) to assess tungsten-induced precipitates and grain boundary characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not show at least a 10–15% increase in yield strength or a statistically significant reduction in creep strain compared to the tungsten-free baseline alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition (2–5 at%) of tungsten into a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the alloy without tungsten.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents along with other elements (each within 5–35 at%), formulated without tungsten.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate 2–5 at% tungsten into the alloy composition during melting and processing.
drafts.conditions: The alloy should be processed under identical heat-treatment conditions and subsequently tested under elevated temperatures (in the range of 700–1000°C) during mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and creep tests).
drafts.structural_mediator: The tungsten addition is expected to promote formation of tungsten-enriched precipitates and refine the grain structure (especially at grain boundaries), which can act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding.
drafts.mechanism: Tungsten’s high melting point and limited solubility can lead to the development of secondary phases that pin grain boundaries and hinder creep mechanisms. This is anticipated to improve the alloy’s yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures by reducing dislocation mobility and grain boundary deformation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit a measurable improvement in high-temperature yield strength (roughly on the order of 15–20% increase compared to the baseline alloy) and a reduction in creep strain under the same elevated-temperature conditions.
drafts.baseline: The identical titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any tungsten addition.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for tungsten concentrations between 2–5 at% and under testing conditions in the elevated temperature range of 700–1000°C. Outside this compositional window and temperature range, the effects are not defined.

Subject both sets to identical annealing treatments and mechanical testing at, for example, 800°C.
measurements: Creep strain over time during high-temperature exposure
